title: Deductive vs inductive reasoning
examples: What is the difference between valid and sound arguments?
Can an argument be valid but not sound?
When should I use inductive reasoning instead of deductive?

explain.say: Today we are looking at two ways of thinking called reasoning.
Deductive reasoning starts with general rules to reach a specific conclusion.
An example is: all men are mortal, and Socrates is a man, so Socrates is mortal.

draw.text: All men are mortal. Socrates is a man. So, Socrates is mortal.

explain.say: Inductive reasoning starts with specific observations to form a general idea.
For instance, you see many swans that are white, so you conclude all swans are white.

draw.text: White swans seen. All swans are white.

explain.say: Validity means the structure is correct, even if the facts are false.

faq.q: What is the difference between validity and truth?
faq.a: Validity is about the structure of the argument, not whether the statements are true. An argument can have a perfect structure but still be based on false starting points.
asks: Does the conclusion have to be true?
Is validity the same as being correct?

faq.q: How do I check if an argument is sound?
faq.a: To check for soundness, you must check two things. First, the argument must be valid in its structure. Second, all of its starting premises must actually be true in the real world.
asks: Do I need true facts for soundness?

faq.q: Can an argument be valid but not sound?
faq.a: Yes, this is very common in logic. If the structure is perfect but one of the starting facts is wrong, the argument is not sound.
asks: If premises are false, is the argument automatically unsound?
What is the relationship between validity and truth?

faq.a: No, inductive reasoning is not guaranteed. It gives us strong probabilities, but it does not prove things with absolute certainty.

faq.q: What is the best way to improve my reasoning skills?
faq.a: Practicing identifying premises and conclusions is very helpful. You should always ask yourself where the evidence comes from.
asks: How do I spot a logical fallacy?
Should I focus more on deduction or induction?

facts: Deductive reasoning moves from general principles to specific conclusions.
Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to general patterns.
An argument is valid if its conclusion must follow from its premises.
An argument is sound if it is both valid and has true premises.

quiz.say: Every time I drop a ball, it falls down. Therefore, all objects fall down.
quiz.show: Ball drops down. All objects fall down.
quiz.why: You observed specific instances (dropping balls) and generalized to a universal rule (all objects).

wrong.1: This is wrong because you started with specific examples, not a general rule.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the pattern observed is very strong, even if it's not a formal proof.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the pattern observed strongly suggests a general rule.

quiz.say: If the argument is valid, what must also be true for it to be sound?

options.show: The premises must be general rules.
options.say: The premises must be general rules.

quiz.why: Soundness is the combination of perfect structure (validity) and factual accuracy (true premises).

wrong.0: This is too restrictive; premises can be specific facts as long as they are true.
wrong.2: While a sound argument has a true conclusion, the definition requires true premises, not just a true outcome.
wrong.3: This is wrong because soundness applies to the structure of the argument, regardless of its type.
